extracted.intended_audience: public commenters, regulated stakeholders, and agency rulewriters participating in federal notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether changes in a final rule are a 'logical outgrowth' of the proposed rule under the Administrative Procedure Act and advising how commenters can preserve or challenge adequate notice. Focuses on legal standard, consequences, and comment strategies to avoid or trigger re-notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical outgrowth doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: The test determines whether the provisions of the final rule logically grow out of the terms of the proposed rule; if so, then the commenters are deemed to have received adequate notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originated in South Terminal Corp. v. EPA (1974). The doctrine balances agency flexibility to respond to comments with the need to give interested parties adequate notice of subjects that could be addressed in a final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable-anticipation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes made in the final rule must be of a type that could have been reasonably anticipated by the public — i.e., a logical outgrowth of the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require that any changes be ones the public could reasonably foresee from the NPRM; unexpected substantive shifts that stakeholders could not have anticipated weigh against finding adequate notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate notice standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule must provide adequate notice to interested parties of the subjects that could be addressed in the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the substantive baseline: if the proposal did not put commenters on notice of the subject matter or specific approach the agency later adopts, the adequacy of the notice is suspect and subject to judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to provide further opportunity for comment when not a logical outgrowth
rubrics_metrics.description: If a change is not a logical outgrowth of the proposal in the NPRM, an agency is required to provide the public with a further opportunity for comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to meet the logical outgrowth test means the agency should issue a second notice with an opportunity for public comment on the new or changed provisions before finalizing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggesting alternatives within the proposal's scope (comment strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggesting alternatives within the proposal's scope creates a stronger record — the agency can adopt them without re-noticing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters who propose concrete alternative approaches that are reasonably related to the proposals in the NPRM make it more likely a court will view the agency's later adoption of those alternatives as a logical outgrowth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying gaps between the proposal and the ideal regulation (comment strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying gaps between the proposal and ideal regulation can prompt re-notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pointing out substantive differences or omissions in the NPRM may induce the agency to re-evaluate and, where appropriate, provide additional notice and an opportunity to comment on significant new directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of comments to preserve logical-outgrowth coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments must be specific about which alternatives they support so the agency can claim their version is a 'logical outgrowth'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vague or general objections are less likely to supply the record needed to justify a later, related change; specificity helps bridge an NPRM proposal and a final rule alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid non-specific mass campaigns (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass campaigns that don't suggest specific alternatives may inadvertently constrain agencies (no logical outgrowth coverage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-volume but non-substantive comment campaigns can fail to create a record showing that the public had notice of particular alternatives, reducing the chance that an adopted change will be treated as a logical outgrowth.
